title: CI/CD Secrets and Pipeline Security: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on keeping secrets out of pipelines, using OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys, locking down runners and branches, securing the software supply chain, and handling untrusted pull request builds.

chapters.title: Secrets and the Pipeline Threat Model
points: Threat model: a pipeline runs code with credentials, so anyone who can change what the pipeline runs can steal what it can reach
Secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) holds secrets centrally with access policy, audit log and rotation; the pipeline fetches at runtime
CI secret variable (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab masked variables) is encrypted at rest and injected as an env var, and log masking only hides the exact string
Comparison: CI variables are simple but copied per repo with no rotation or audit; a secret store gives central control, short TTLs and dynamic secrets
Never echo secrets, bake them into images or artifacts, or put them in command-line args; transformed values (base64, split) bypass masking

chapters.title: OIDC Federation Instead of Long-Lived Keys
points: Long-lived cloud keys stored in CI never expire, leak through logs and forks, and need manual rotation; OIDC removes them
Mechanism: the CI provider issues a short-lived signed JWT per job, the cloud verifies it against the provider's public keys and exchanges it for temporary credentials
Token claims to trust: iss, aud, sub (repo, branch or environment), plus ref and workflow; the cloud trust policy matches on these

AWS example: IAM role trusted by token.actions.githubusercontent.com, condition sub = repo:org/app:environment:prod, workflow needs permissions: id-token: write and uses aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume
Mistake: a trust policy with wildcard sub (repo:org/*) or no aud check lets any repo or fork assume the role; pin repo plus branch or environment

chapters.title: Runners, Branches and Environments
points: Least-privilege workflow token: set permissions: contents: read at the top and grant write scopes only on the job that needs them
Hosted runners are ephemeral and clean per job; self-hosted runners persist state and sit inside your network, so use them only for trusted private repos, ideally ephemeral or just-in-time
Protected branches: require pull request review, passing status checks, signed commits and no force pushes, so unreviewed code cannot reach the deploy branch
Protected environments (prod): required reviewers, branch restrictions and environment-scoped secrets, so a job gets prod secrets only after approval on an allowed branch
Mistake: one broad secret shared by all branches, admins bypassing protection, or a self-hosted runner on a public repo (any fork PR runs code on your machine)

chapters.title: Supply-Chain Security: Pinning, SBOM and Sigstore
points: Supply-chain risks: compromised dependency, typosquatting, dependency confusion, tampered build action or image, poisoned build output

Pin dependencies: commit lockfiles with hashes and install with npm ci or pip install --require-hashes; pin third-party actions and base images to a full commit SHA or image digest, not a mutable tag like @v3 or :latest
SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) is a machine-readable inventory of every component in an artifact; generate with syft and scan with grype to find vulnerable versions
Sigstore signing: cosign sign with keyless OIDC identity, signature logged in the Rekor transparency log; verify with cosign verify --certificate-identity and --certificate-oidc-issuer before deploy
Comparison: SBOM says what is inside, a signature says who built it, provenance (SLSA attestation) says how it was built; use all three, and a signature proves origin, not safety

chapters.title: Untrusted Pull Request Builds
points: Fork PR code is untrusted: it can edit the workflow, scripts and tests, so running it with secrets is remote code execution
GitHub pull_request from forks runs with no secrets and a read-only token; pull_request_target runs in the base repo context with secrets, so it is dangerous with PR code
Pwn request: pull_request_target plus actions/checkout of the PR head and running its code gives the attacker your secrets and write token

Safe pattern: build and test untrusted code in a no-secret pull_request workflow, pass results as artifacts, and let a separate trusted workflow_run job comment or deploy; require maintainer approval for first-time contributors
Script injection: never put untrusted fields like github.event.pull_request.title or branch names directly in run: scripts; pass them via env: and quote the variable

chapters.title: Pipeline Security Cheat Sheet
points: Secrets: store in a secret store, prefer short-lived or dynamic secrets, scope per environment, never print them, rotate on leak
OIDC: permissions: id-token: write, trust policy pinned to repo plus branch or environment, aud checked, no static cloud keys
Hardening: permissions: contents: read by default, ephemeral runners, protected branches (reviews, checks, no force push), protected environments with reviewers
Supply chain: lockfile with hashes, actions by SHA, images by digest, syft SBOM, grype scan, cosign sign and verify
Fork PRs: use pull_request, never run PR head code under pull_request_target, pass untrusted values via env, require approval for first-time contributors
